variants.name: EF Core concurrency token
variants.implementation_notes: EF Core implements optimistic concurrency with concurrency tokens: mark one property with [Timestamp] (SQL Server rowversion), [ConcurrencyCheck] or IsConcurrencyToken(), and EF appends it to the WHERE clause of every UPDATE/DELETE it generates; when zero rows match, SaveChanges()/SaveChangesAsync() throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. DbUpdateConcurrencyException.Entries plus Entry.GetDatabaseValuesAsync() and OriginalValues.SetValues() provide the current, original and database value sets needed to merge instead of overwrite. Databases without a native rowversion (SQLite) need an application-managed token that is reassigned on every write.
pitfalls: Retrying without refreshing OriginalValues throws again forever - the original token is what the WHERE clause compares.
An application-managed token (Guid/int) must be reassigned on every write path; a SaveChanges override or interceptor is the only place that guarantees it.
Deleting a concurrently modified row also throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, while insert conflicts surface as provider-specific unique-constraint exceptions - handle both shapes.

variants.name: DataSet / DataAdapter original-values guard
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-ORM realization keeps the token in the DataSet: the update command's WHERE clause is bound to the original values (SqlParameter.SourceVersion = DataRowVersion.Original), so the UPDATE matches only if the row still holds the values that were read; a zero RecordsAffected on the RowUpdated event marks the violation, which the handler records with DataRow.RowError and UpdateStatus. Choose it when the data layer is still DataSet-based; EF Core's token is the better default otherwise.
pitfalls: Comparing every column (or forgetting the @old parameters) makes the WHERE clause fragile and slow; a dedicated timestamp/rowversion column is the cheaper token.
RecordsAffected is 0 for a deleted row too: distinguish deletion from update before declaring a conflict.
Stored procedures that suppress row counts (SET NOCOUNT ON) make RecordsAffected report -1 and defeat the check.
